The Ethiopian Empire, also called Abyssinia, was the Christian monarchy of the Ethiopian highlands from 1270 to 1974. It began when Yekuno Amlak overthrew the Zagwe dynasty, the line of Lalibela, and founded the Solomonic dynasty, which claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba.

It saw itself as heir to Aksum, whose kings had adopted Christianity in the 300s, and its church kept Ge'ez as its holy language.

  • 1300s and 1400s: strong emperors such as Amda Seyon and Zara Yaqob expanded the realm and reformed the church.
  • 1529 to 1543: Imam Ahmad of Adal overran most of the highlands. Portuguese musketeers helped the Ethiopians defeat him in 1543.
  • 1636: Fasilides made Gondar the capital, where castles still stand.
  • 1769 to 1855: the Era of the Princes, when regional lords held real power and emperors were figureheads.
  • From 1855: Tewodros II, Yohannes IV and Menelik II rebuilt central power. Menelik conquered lands to the south, founded Addis Ababa in 1886 and beat Italy at the Battle of Adwa in 1896.

Adwa kept Ethiopia independent through the Scramble for Africa. Italy invaded again in 1935 and occupied the country from 1936 to 1941, while Haile Selassie lived in exile; British and Ethiopian forces drove the Italians out. Eritrea was joined to Ethiopia in 1952. In 1974, after famine and protests, a military committee, the Derg, deposed Haile Selassie and ended the monarchy.
